heading: The Holocaust
body: The Nazi regime murdered around six million Jews — roughly two-thirds of the Jewish population of Europe. This was not a by-product of the war. It was a state policy, pursued with the resources of a modern industrial country, and in its final phase pursued even where doing so cost the war effort directly, diverting trains and men from a collapsing front to keep the killing going. It happened in stages, and the stages matter because they show a society being brought along. Exclusion came first: from 1933, Jews were driven from the civil service, the professions and the universities; the Nuremberg Laws of 1935 stripped citizenship and criminalised marriage; businesses were expropriated. In November 1938, Kristallnacht saw synagogues burned and thousands of Jewish men sent to camps, with the police standing by. Emigration was the official aim, and most countries, including Britain and the United States, sharply limited how many they would admit. The invasion of Poland in 1939 brought two million Jews under German control and produced the ghettos — sealed districts in Warsaw, Łódź and elsewhere where hundreds of thousands were confined in conditions engineered to kill by starvation and disease, and did. The invasion of the Soviet Union in June 1941 began mass murder. Einsatzgruppen — mobile killing units following the army — shot Jewish communities at the edges of their own towns, often with assistance from local auxiliaries and the knowledge and cooperation of the regular army. Around a million and a half people were killed this way, a phase now often called the Holocaust by bullets, and Babi Yar outside Kyiv, where over 33,000 people were shot in two days in September 1941, stands for all of it. Shooting was then judged inefficient and psychologically hard on the killers. At Wannsee in January 1942 senior officials met to coordinate what was already under way — the conference organised the killing, it did not initiate it. Six extermination camps operated in occupied Poland: Chełmno, Bełżec, Sobibór and Treblinka, built for killing and almost nothing else, and Majdanek and Auschwitz-Birkenau, which combined killing with slave labour. Around 1.1 million people died at Auschwitz alone. Victims arrived by rail from across Europe, were selected on the platform, and most were dead within hours. Jews were the central target but not the only one. Around 3.3 million Soviet prisoners of war died in German captivity, most deliberately starved. Between a quarter and half a million Roma and Sinti were murdered. The T4 programme killed some 200,000 disabled people in Germany itself, and provided the personnel and methods later used in the camps. Poles, gay men, Jehovah's Witnesses and political prisoners died in large numbers. There was resistance — the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising in 1943, revolts at Treblinka and Sobibór, partisan units, and individuals across occupied Europe who hid people at the risk of their own lives. There was also extensive collaboration. Both are part of the record, and a history that reports only one of them is not telling the truth.

heading: Occupation, collaboration, resistance, and the home fronts
body: Most Europeans experienced the war as occupation rather than combat, and occupation varied enormously by where you were on the regime's racial hierarchy. Denmark kept its government and its king. France was split between a German-occupied north and the Vichy regime in the south, which collaborated, passed its own antisemitic laws unprompted, and delivered Jews for deportation. Poland was treated as a colony to be emptied: its universities closed, its elite systematically murdered, its population scheduled for displacement. The occupied Soviet territories were treated worse still. Resistance existed everywhere and was rarely simple. It ran from intelligence-gathering and escape lines to sabotage and, in Yugoslavia and parts of the Soviet Union, to full partisan armies holding territory. It was militarily useful mainly at moments of leverage — French railway sabotage around Normandy delayed German reinforcement measurably. It also invited reprisal: villages such as Lidice in Czechoslovakia and Oradour-sur-Glane in France were destroyed and their inhabitants murdered in retaliation, which was the point of the policy. Occupied populations were rarely divided cleanly into resisters and collaborators; the great majority simply tried to survive, and after the war every occupied country constructed a national memory that flattered itself somewhat. The home fronts were transformed. Total war meant the whole economy was directed at production, and in Britain and the Soviet Union this went further than in Germany, which was slower to mobilise fully and never conscripted women on the same scale — partly for ideological reasons, and partly because it was extracting forced labour from occupied Europe instead. Some eight million foreign workers, many of them effectively slaves, were working in Germany by 1944. Women entered industry, agriculture and the armed forces in unprecedented numbers. The Soviet Union put women into combat roles including fighter aviation and sniping; Britain and the United States kept them out of direct combat but relied on them for aircraft production, agriculture, anti-aircraft crews, transport and codebreaking. The post-war attempt to return everyone to pre-war roles largely succeeded in the short term and did not survive the generation. Rationing, blackout, evacuation of children from cities, conscription of labour as well as soldiers, propaganda and censorship were the texture of daily life. The United States, uniquely among the major combatants, fought the entire war without bombing of its own territory and with its industry expanding — it finished the war with roughly half the world's manufacturing output, which is the single fact that most shaped the peace. It also interned around 120,000 Japanese Americans, most of them citizens, on no individual evidence — a decision the American government formally apologised and paid reparations for four decades later.

heading: The Mediterranean: North Africa, Italy, and the war's first Allied turn
body: The Mediterranean campaign is often treated as a sideshow, and it was not one — it was where British and American forces learned to fight, and where the first Allied victories came. Italy entered the war in June 1940, when France was already beaten, and promptly demonstrated that its ambitions exceeded its army. An invasion of Greece from Albania in October was thrown back by the Greeks; an advance into Egypt was routed by a much smaller British force. Germany bailed its ally out on both counts, conquering Greece and Yugoslavia in April 1941 and sending Rommel and the Afrika Korps to Libya. The desert war that followed swung back and forth across a thousand miles of coast for two years, because both sides advanced until they outran their supplies and then were pushed back. Its decisive moment came at El Alamein in Egypt in October and November 1942, where a British Commonwealth army under Montgomery, materially superior and reading Rommel's supply signals through Ultra, broke the Axis line. Churchill's remark that it marked the end of the beginning is the fairest summary: it was the first clear British land victory over the German army and it ended the threat to Suez. Days later, Operation Torch landed American and British forces in Morocco and Algeria, putting the Axis in North Africa between two armies. The campaign ended in Tunisia in May 1943 with the surrender of roughly a quarter of a million Axis troops — a loss comparable to Stalingrad, three months later, and much less remembered. Sicily was invaded in July 1943 and the political effect was immediate: Mussolini was deposed by his own Grand Council and arrested, and in September Italy surrendered and changed sides. Germany responded by occupying the country, disarming the Italian army, rescuing Mussolini to head a puppet state in the north, and fighting for every mile of a peninsula whose mountain spine and rivers favour the defender absolutely. The result was eighteen months of grinding attrition at Monte Cassino, at the Anzio beachhead that was contained almost as soon as it landed, and up a series of fortified lines. Rome did not fall until June 1944, two days before Normandy, which is why almost nobody remembers the date. The strategic argument over Italy was never settled. It tied down German divisions and secured Mediterranean shipping. It also consumed Allied divisions in the least favourable terrain available, and Churchill's description of the theatre as Europe's soft underbelly did not survive contact with the Apennines.

heading: 1944 to 1945: Normandy, the Bulge, and the fall of Germany
body: The Western Allies had been building towards a landing in France for two years, and on 6 June 1944 they made it. Around 156,000 men went ashore on five Normandy beaches in a single day, supported by airborne landings inland, an armada of some 7,000 vessels and near-total air superiority. The logistics were as remarkable as the assault: two prefabricated harbours were towed across the Channel in sections, and a fuel pipeline was laid on the seabed. What made it work was as much deception as force. Operation Fortitude convinced the German command that the real landing would come at the Pas de Calais, using fictitious formations, controlled double agents and false radio traffic — and, crucially, kept convincing them for weeks after D-Day, so that powerful German reserves sat waiting for an invasion that never came. The Normandy fighting was harder than the landing. The bocage — small fields divided by ancient earth banks and hedges — suited defence and cost the Allies dearly through June and July. The breakout came at the end of July, and in August German forces were caught in the Falaise pocket and destroyed. Paris was liberated on 25 August, and Allied armies then advanced so fast that they outran their fuel. An attempt to bounce the Rhine at Arnhem in September, Operation Market Garden, failed at the last bridge. In December Germany mounted one last offensive, through the Ardennes again, aiming to split the Allied armies and retake Antwerp. The Battle of the Bulge achieved surprise in bad weather that grounded Allied aircraft, created a deep salient, and then stalled for want of fuel — some German units were relying on capturing Allied dumps. When the skies cleared it was destroyed from the air. It cost Germany the reserves it would need to defend the Rhine, and it was the last time the German army attacked in the west. The end came quickly. The Rhine was crossed in March 1945. In February, Roosevelt, Churchill and Stalin had met at Yalta and agreed the shape of the post-war world, including occupation zones and Soviet entry into the war against Japan — an agreement much criticised later for conceding Eastern Europe, though in practical terms the Red Army was already standing on most of it. American and Soviet troops met at the Elbe on 25 April. The Red Army fought into Berlin at enormous cost. Hitler killed himself in his bunker on 30 April, and Germany surrendered unconditionally on 7 May, with effect from the 8th — a day the Soviet Union marks on the 9th, because of the time zone in which the second signing took place.

heading: The end in the Pacific, and the argument about the bomb
body: By mid-1945 Japan had lost its navy, its merchant fleet, its air force and its access to the raw materials the war had been started to secure. It had not surrendered. Okinawa, fought from April to June, was the last island battle and the bloodiest: around 12,000 American dead, roughly 100,000 Japanese defenders killed, and somewhere between 100,000 and 150,000 Okinawan civilians dead, many by mass suicide encouraged by the army. American planners read Okinawa as a preview of the home islands and produced casualty estimates for an invasion that ranged widely and were all appalling. Alongside it, conventional bombing had already devastated Japan. The firebombing of Tokyo on the night of 9 to 10 March 1945 killed something like 100,000 people and burned out sixteen square miles of the city — more deaths than either atomic bomb caused on the day. The Potsdam Declaration in July demanded unconditional surrender and was rejected. On 6 August an atomic bomb was dropped on Hiroshima, killing around 70,000 people immediately and roughly twice that by the end of the year as burns and radiation sickness took their toll. On 8 August the Soviet Union declared war and invaded Manchuria, destroying Japan's largest remaining field army in days. On 9 August a second bomb was dropped on Nagasaki, killing around 40,000 immediately. Japan announced surrender on 15 August, and the formal instrument was signed on 2 September. Whether the bombs were necessary is the most argued question of the war, and an honest guide sets out the positions rather than picking one. The traditional case is that Japan's government was not seeking surrender on acceptable terms, that an invasion would have killed vastly more people on both sides, including Japanese civilians, and that the alternative to the bombs was not peace but a blockade and firebombing campaign that was already killing on a comparable scale month by month. The revisionist case is that Japan was already beaten and knew it, that a guarantee about the Emperor's position — which was granted in the end anyway — might have secured surrender without the bombs, and that the demonstration of the weapon to the Soviet Union was among the motives. A third line, increasingly weighted by historians with access to Japanese records, holds that the Soviet declaration of war mattered at least as much as the bombs in the Japanese cabinet's deliberations, because it extinguished the last hope of a negotiated peace mediated by Moscow. What is not in dispute is what the weapons did to the people under them, and that the world has lived since inside the question those two days opened.

heading: The cost, and the difficulty of counting it
body: Estimates of the war's death toll run from about 70 million to about 85 million people — somewhere around three per cent of everyone alive. The range is wide because the counting is genuinely hard. Records were destroyed with the states that kept them; famine and disease deaths caused by the war are counted by some authorities and not others; the Bengal famine of 1943, in which perhaps three million died under wartime British administration, appears in some totals and not in others; and several governments had reasons to revise their figures afterwards. What is clear is the distribution. The Soviet Union lost around 27 million people. China lost somewhere between 15 and 20 million. Poland lost about six million, close to a fifth of its entire pre-war population and the highest proportion of any country. Germany lost six to eight million, Japan around three million. Britain lost about 450,000 and the United States about 420,000 — real losses, and one to two orders of magnitude smaller in proportion than what was suffered in the east. Any account that gives the Western Allies the leading role in the human cost has the arithmetic wrong. The other decisive change is who died. In the First World War the great majority of the dead were soldiers. In the Second, the majority were civilians — killed by deliberate murder, by bombing, by siege and by starvation. That inversion is the most important single fact about how war changed between 1918 and 1945, and it is why the legal instruments that followed concentrate on the protection of civilians. Beyond the dead: some 11 million displaced persons were in camps in Europe at the war's end, people with no home or country to return to. Millions more were forcibly moved in the following years, as German populations were expelled westward from Poland and Czechoslovakia and borders were redrawn across the region. Cities across Europe and Japan lay in ruins. Two-thirds of European Jewry was gone, and communities that had existed for a thousand years no longer existed at all. There is one number worth carrying out of any account of this war, and it is not a total. It is the observation that these figures are made of individuals, and that the mind cannot hold six million or twenty-seven million as a quantity. Historians who work on the period are nearly unanimous that the correct response to the scale is not to try to feel it all, which is impossible, but to keep hold of the fact that each unit in it was a person with a name — which is precisely why the memorials that work best read out names rather than reporting sums.

heading: What the war left
body: The institutions of the modern world were built in the eighteen months around the war's end by people who had just watched the previous arrangements fail completely, and reading them as responses to specific failures is the fastest way to understand why they are shaped as they are. The United Nations, chartered in 1945, was designed to correct the League of Nations' weaknesses: it would include the great powers, and it would have a Security Council with enforcement powers. The veto given to the five permanent members is routinely criticised as the reason it cannot act against them, and it was also the price of their joining at all — a body they could not veto is a body they would not have signed. Bretton Woods created the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank on the judgment that the economic disorder of the 1930s had produced the politics of the 1930s. The Nuremberg and Tokyo trials established that individuals could be prosecuted for crimes against humanity and that following orders was not a defence — a genuine break with prior international law, and open to the charge of victors' justice, which the defence made and the tribunals did not fully answer. The Genocide Convention and the Universal Declaration of Human Rights followed in 1948, the revised Geneva Conventions in 1949. The word genocide itself was coined in 1944 by the lawyer Raphael Lemkin, who had lost most of his family, because he judged that a crime without a name could not be prosecuted. The alliance that won the war dissolved almost immediately into the Cold War. Germany was divided along the occupation zones and stayed divided for forty-four years. The Marshall Plan rebuilt Western Europe with American money on the explicit reasoning that the punitive settlement of 1919 had helped produce Hitler. NATO followed in 1949 and the Warsaw Pact in 1955, and the line between them ran through the middle of the continent until 1989. The European empires did not survive their own victory. Britain and France had been shown to be defeatable, had drawn heavily on colonial troops and resources with promises attached, and were too exhausted to hold what they claimed. India became independent in 1947 and the rest followed over two decades. European integration began in 1951 with a coal and steel community whose stated purpose was to bind French and German industry so tightly together that another war between them would be materially impossible — an aim that has, so far, held. And the war remains the central moral reference point of Western political argument, invoked constantly and often carelessly. That is worth noticing in itself. Every nation that fought remembers a somewhat different war, shaped by what it needed to believe afterwards, and the discipline of history is largely the work of putting those memories back against the evidence.
